newsitem.title: USA: Mideast summit may give Dole chance to hit Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Mideast summit may give Dole chance to hit Clinton.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

The uncertain conclusion of the Middle East summit may give Republican Bob Dole an opening to attack President Bill Clinton in their campaign debate on Sunday, but most voters seem unconcerned over foreign policy.
Two days of high-level talks in Washington gave Clinton yet another opportunity to dominate the air waves and look presidential while pushing Dole into the background.

But the summit failed to produce any agreements resolving Israeli-Palestinian disputes, and reaction to Clinton's diplomacy was mixed. A Washington Post editorial called the meeting a "disaster". The Los Angeles Times said it provided the parties with a "valuable nudge" in the direction of peace.

"The summit does give Dole an opening to argue that Clinton's foreign policy is adrift. But this is not very high on anybody's agenda right now," said David Birdsell, a political scientist at Baruch College in New York.
"Dole has to emphasise that he has the credibility that Clinton lacks to assume the mantle of a sage senior statesman. So far, he's been unable to do that," Birdsell said.

That is not for lack of trying. Even while the summit was still in progress, Dole took the unusual step of attacking it as "photo-op diplomacy" while Newt Gingrich, Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, accused Clinton of a failure of leadership.
"It is very unfortunate to see this kind of lack of thought, lack of structure ... lack of planning and lack of systematic leadership," Gingrich said.

Clinton and Dole face off in the first of two presidential debates on Sunday evening. With less than five weeks to Election Day on Nov. 5, the debates may give Dole his last real opportunity to cut into Clinton's wide lead in the polls.
The Middle East may well come up in the debate and, if it does, Dole will probably argue that the summit was just the latest example of Clinton's foreign policy coming unstuck in crucial areas.
His position is that Clinton's much ballyhooed successes in brokering peace deals in Bosnia and Ireland are as fragile as the Middle East peace of which he is so proud.
"Dole should try to emphasise the Middle East as an example of how Clinton is not competent at governance," said Robert Holsworth, a political scientist at Virginia Commonwealth University.
"But Dole's bigger problem is that he has yet to convince the public he should be taken seriously as a fully credible presidential contender," Holsworth said.

There may be little mileage for Dole in the Middle East issue. In a recent Reuters poll, voters ranked foreign policy ninth most important issue out of a possible 10, ahead of only abortion and behind the economy, education, the environment, health and welfare reform among others.
The Middle East is most important to Jewish Americans. But a Reuters poll this week found 83 percent of that group in Clinton's corner.
Dole has reacted by trying to become even more pro-Israeli than Clinton, forging a close alliance with the ruling right-wing Likud party.
While still in the Senate, Dole supported a resolution opposed both by the administration and the former Israeli Labour Party government to move the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem.
This week, he warned Clinton not to apply any pressure on Israel to make concessions.

"I was disappointed that President Clinton's statement did not include an unequivocal condemnation of the recent violence," the Republican challenger said after meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday.
But many Jews regard Clinton as one of the most pro-Israel presidents ever and are alarmed by the growing power of the evangelical Christian wing of the Republican Party.
